rationale: A wins because it stays inside the evidence and turns weak launch facts into reportable questions instead of decorating the holes. Its “How big does a purchase have to be before Pay by Bank beats a card?” is a real analysis frame with the correct kill switch: “Without the fee schedule this angle cannot be pitched.” B has usable bones, but “FedNow just got its most significant commercial test” and “Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes” are how plausible context turns into unearned claims.
gaps_in_A: Refusing “Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network” as “duplicate” throws away a possible company-strategy lens; it should be conditional on Plaid proving strategic intent, not dismissed as the same card-network story.

“A flat fee is worse than a percentage on small tickets” is too absolute without the actual card fee stack and flat fee; the angle correctly asks for the schedule, but the claim should be framed as a hypothesis.
“journalist-fit-check for the counterposition angle” is a little narrow; the FedNow infrastructure angle could also be fit-checked if pitched as a rail-adoption data point with reach caveats.
gaps_in_B: “FedNow just got its most significant commercial test” is an unsupported superlative. The update says FedNow rails are used; it does not prove significance.
“FedNow has been live for roughly three years” and “standing open question” import outside context the model was not given, then treat it as a peg.
“Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes” and “competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen” are invented company-history and competitor claims.
“Merchants using Plaid's Pay by Bank report fees up to 70% lower” quietly upgrades “Plaid says early merchants see” into merchant-sourced proof. That changes the evidentiary footing.
